name: landrun
desc: Lightweight, secure sandbox for running Linux processes using Landlock LSM
why: Runs processes under Landlock LSM restrictions, a good door into kernel sandboxing you rarely see.

brief.what_it_is: Landrun is a command-line sandbox for Linux. You put it in front of any command, such as `landrun --rox /usr --ro /etc --connect-tcp 443 nc kernel.org 443`, and it runs that command under Landlock restrictions. You list which paths the process may read, write, or execute, and which TCP/UDP ports it may bind or connect to. The command's output is the same as it would be unsandboxed, and any access outside the rules is denied by the kernel. It is written in Go and needs no root privileges.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a practical way to sandbox any command with fine-grained filesystem and network controls, with "No root. No containers. No SELinux/AppArmor configs." It describes itself as "Think firejail, but with kernel-level security and minimal overhead."
brief.how_it_works: Landrun wraps the Landlock Linux Security Module, which lets an unprivileged process restrict itself and its future children. It builds a ruleset from the --ro, --rox, --rw, --rwx, --bind-tcp, --connect-tcp, --bind-udp, --connect-udp and --unix flags, then applies it before running the target command. The README targets Landlock ABI v10 by default and uses the go-landlock package (v0.10.0). Its --best-effort mode falls back to whatever ABI the running kernel supports. The README also covers IPC scoping for abstract UNIX sockets and signals, which is on by default, and audit logging of denials.

brief.install_notes: Requires Linux kernel 5.13 or later with Landlock enabled. TCP restrictions need kernel 6.7 or later, and UDP restrictions need 7.2 or later (ABI v10). Building from source needs Go 1.24 or later: clone the repo, run `go build -o landrun cmd/landrun/main.go`, then copy the binary to /usr/local/bin. Distro packages are listed: Arch AUR (landrun and landrun-git), Slackware via SlackBuilds, and `sudo apt install landrun` on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Debian forky. No root is needed to run the sandbox itself. Systems without Landlock enabled will need the kernel config checked. Most real use will need --best-effort on older kernels, and paths such as /usr, /usr/lib, and /lib64 usually have to be granted explicitly. There is no first-run configuration. A systemd unit example is included in the README.
brief.standout: Landrun brings Landlock, a kernel feature most people never touch, to a simple command-line wrapper. Users get path- and port-level restrictions with no root, no container, and no policy language to write. The README also documents Landlock's newer features, including UDP port control, IPC scoping, and pathname UNIX socket control, with a kernel-version table to match.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release dates, changelog, or last-commit information, and I did not open the repository's releases or commit history. Signs of ongoing packaging are that it is in Ubuntu 26.04 and Debian forky and has several AUR and SlackBuild maintainers. It targets recent kernel features such as ABI v10 and Linux 7.2 UDP restrictions. The README has a Contributing section that invites pull requests.
brief.caveats: Strict mode fails on kernels below the requested ABI, so most users will need --best-effort. TCP restrictions do not apply to Multipath TCP, and since Go 1.24 net.Listen defaults to MPTCP, so Go servers may not be restrictable (kernel bug landlock-lsm/linux#54). Files opened before sandboxing are not restricted. Shared libraries need exec permission, so the rules are not always as minimal as they look. Linux only. The README does not state a license in what I read. It also links an article titled "Binaries are not trustworthy", which suggests building from source.
quotes: Think firejail, but with kernel-level security and minimal overhead.
No root. No containers. No SELinux/AppArmor configs.
Landlock is an access-control system that enables processes to securely restrict themselves and their future children.

entry.title: landrun
entry.tldr: Put landrun in front of any Linux command and the kernel itself restricts which files and network ports it can touch, with no root or containers.
entry.deeper_look:
Landrun is a small command-line wrapper around Landlock, a Linux security module that lets an unprivileged process restrict itself and its future children. You list what the command may read, write, or execute, and which TCP or UDP ports it may bind or connect to. Landrun builds that ruleset, applies it, and then runs your command. Anything outside the rules is denied by the kernel, and the command's output is otherwise unchanged.

The README's pitch is "No root. No containers. No SELinux/AppArmor configs." and it describes the tool as "Think firejail, but with kernel-level security and minimal overhead." It is written in Go on top of the go-landlock package.

The interesting part is the idea underneath. With no flags at all, `landrun ls` runs in a maximum-restriction jail, and you then add permissions one at a time until the program works. The denial errors teach you what a program actually touches: which libraries it loads, which config it reads, which ports it opens. The README suggests running under strace when the errors are unclear. Landrun also covers newer Landlock features such as UDP port control, IPC scoping, and pathname UNIX socket control, with a kernel-version table to match.
entry.install:
brew install landrun
# Needs Linux kernel 5.13+ with Landlock enabled. TCP rules need kernel 6.7+, UDP rules need 7.2+.
# Alternative: go install github.com/zouuup/landrun/cmd/landrun@latest (Go 1.24+)

try_this.what_happens: With no rules given, landrun applies maximum restrictions, so you see the command running in a jail where it can reach almost nothing.
Runs nc with exec access to /usr and permission to connect only to TCP port 443.
Traces the sandboxed ls to show which accesses are being denied, the README's suggested debugging step.

entry.whats_unique: It turns Landlock, a kernel feature most people never touch, into a one-line wrapper with path and port rules. There is no root, no container, and no policy language to learn.
entry.caveats: Linux only, strict mode fails on kernels older than the requested Landlock ABI so most people will need --best-effort, and Go servers may escape TCP rules because of a Multipath TCP quirk.
